usage: The first thing people ask if you limp in or hold an injured spot; 어디 = 'where (on the body)'.
Be careful not to get hurt
다치지 않게 = 'so as not to get hurt'; standard warning at the gym, on icy streets, or near construction.
크게 다치다 = 'to be seriously injured'; 크게 (lit. 'big-ly') is the default adverb for the severity of an injury.
다친 데 = 'the hurt spot'; the caring check-in right after someone trips, crashes, or gets in a fender-bender.
examples: 손을 다쳤어요.
I hurt my hand.
Simplest frame: body part + 을/를 + 다치다. The hurt body part is the object, not the subject.
축구하다가 무릎을 다쳤어요.
I hurt my knee while playing soccer.
V-다가 = 'while doing X, (something happened)'; the most common way to set up how an injury occurred.
넘어져서 손목을 좀 다쳤는데 병원 가야 할까요?
I fell and hurt my wrist a bit — should I go to the hospital?
Real clinic-decision moment; 넘어지다 = to fall over, and naming 손목 (wrist) routes you to 정형외과 (orthopedics).
nuance: 다치다 is the everyday verb for getting physically injured — bumps, cuts, sprains, breaks — and crucially the injured body part takes 을/를, not 이/가 (무릎을 다쳤어요, not 무릎이). Although it translates as 'to hurt', it behaves like an intransitive 'to GET hurt' aimed at yourself, so you cannot use it to mean 'I hurt someone else' — that is 다치게 하다 or 상처를 입히다. The nearest neighbor is 아프다, and the dividing line matters: 다치다 is the one-time event of getting injured (넘어져서 다쳤어요), while 아프다 is the lingering pain or sickness that follows (지금도 아파요). It pairs habitually with 크게 다치다 (badly hurt), 살짝/조금 다치다 (slightly hurt), and 다친 데 (the injured spot). At a hospital, 다치다 plus the exact body part (발목, 허리, 손목) gets you to the right department fast.

mistakes: Using 아프다 when you mean an injury — 아프다 is 'it hurts / I'm sick' (a state), but 다치다 is the act of getting injured (an event). Say '넘어져서 다쳤어요' for the injury, then '지금도 아파요' for the pain that remains.
Marking the body part with 이/가 — it's 무릎을 다쳤어요 (object 을), not 무릎이 다쳤어요. The body part is what you injure, so it takes 을/를.
Trying to say 'I hurt my friend' with 다치다 — 친구를 다쳤어요 is wrong because 다치다 is about getting hurt yourself. Use 친구를 다치게 했어요 ('I caused my friend to get hurt').

usage: THE phrase to send a sick coworker or friend; the honorific 나으세요 is warmer and more polite than 빨리 나아요.
Are you over your cold now?
다 낫다 = 'to be fully healed'; 다 = 'all/completely', the natural check-in after someone was sick.
It won't get better even though I take medicine
Useful at a clinic to say a remedy isn't working; 안 나아요 keeps the ㅅ dropped before the vowel.
상처가 낫다 = 'a wound heals'; 잘 = 'well/nicely', the reassuring report after a cut or surgery site closes up.
examples: 감기가 나았어요.
My cold got better.
Core pattern: the illness is the SUBJECT (감기가) — you don't heal something, the sickness heals on its own.
약 먹으니까 감기가 금방 나았어요.
I took the medicine and the cold got better quickly.
ㅅ-irregular in action: 낫 + 았어요 → 나았어요 (the ㅅ drops). 금방 = 'in no time'. Don't write 낳았어요 (gave birth).
푹 쉬면 곧 나을 거예요, 너무 무리하지 마세요.
If you rest well you'll soon get better, so don't overdo it.
푹 쉬다 = 'to rest fully'; the classic comforting send-off pairing 나을 거예요 with 무리하지 마세요.
nuance: 낫다 means an illness or wound heals, and it is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ disappears before a vowel (나아요, 나았어요, 나을, 나으세요) but stays before a consonant (낫습니다, 낫고, 낫지). It is intransitive — the cold or the cut is the subject (감기가 나았어요, 상처가 나았어요) — so you never 'heal something' with it; for that you'd use 치료하다 (to treat) or 고치다 (to cure/fix). The big trap for everyone, native and learner alike, is the homophone cluster: 낫다 'heal', 낳다 'give birth', and 났다 (from 나다, 'broke out/occurred') all sound like [낟따] but mean totally different things, so 나았어요 (got better) must never be spelled 낳았어요 (gave birth). Note 낫다 also has a second meaning, 'to be better/preferable' (이게 더 나아요 = this one's better), which shares the exact same conjugation. It collocates with 빨리/금방/곧 낫다 (heal fast/soon) and 다 낫다 (fully heal).

Keeping the ㅅ before a vowel — it's 나아요/나았어요/나을, NOT 낫아요/낫았어요. The ㅅ only survives before consonants (낫습니다, 낫고).
Making it transitive like English 'heal it' — 감기를 나았어요 is wrong; the illness is the subject, so it's 감기가 나았어요. To 'cure' something actively, use 치료하다 or 고치다.

usage: The single most useful sprain phrase — say it at any 정형외과 or pharmacy; 발목 (ankle) is the default body part.
I tweaked it / wrenched it slightly
삐끗하다 is the casual everyday word for a minor twist of the ankle or back, lighter than a full 삐다.
붓다 (to swell) is the symptom that follows a sprain; '삐어서 부었어요' tells a doctor the whole story.
접질리다 is a near-synonym for a wrenched/twisted joint; good to recognize when a Korean uses it instead of 삐다.
examples: 발목을 삐었어요.
I sprained my ankle.
Bare-bones report; 삐다 almost always takes 발목 (ankle) or 손목 (wrist) as the object with 을/를.
계단에서 내려오다가 발목을 삐었어요.
I sprained my ankle coming down the stairs.
V-다가 sets up the mid-action accident; 내려오다 = to come down. A textbook way to explain how it happened.
어제 발목을 삐었는데 오늘 더 부어서 병원에 가려고요.
I sprained my ankle yesterday but it's more swollen today, so I'm going to the hospital.
Real decision moment chaining 삐다 + 붓다 + clinic; -(으)려고요 = 'I intend to', softens the announcement.
nuance: 삐다 is the plain everyday verb for spraining a joint, overwhelmingly collocating with 발목 (ankle) and 손목 (wrist), with the joint as the object (발목을 삐다). Because a sprain is a sudden event you report after the fact, it lives most naturally in the past/result form 삐었어요 rather than the present. Mind the boundaries with its neighbors: 접질리다 also means to wrench/twist a joint and overlaps heavily, while the casual 삐끗하다 covers a milder 'tweak'; most importantly, 삐다 (a sprain — soft tissue) is NOT 부러지다 (a bone fracture), so a clinic needs to hear which one. There's no Sino-Korean root here — it's a native Korean word. For a doctor, 발목을 삐었어요 plus 부었어요 (it's swollen) communicates the whole problem; standard first-aid is to 얼음찜질하다 (ice it).

Using the present tense 삐어요 to report an injury that already happened — say 삐었어요 (past), since you're describing a completed event. Present 삐어요 sounds like a general 'one tends to sprain it'.
Marking the joint with 이/가 — it's 발목을 삐었어요 (object 을), not 발목이 삐었어요. You sprain the ankle, so it takes 을/를.

usage: What the doctor says about a rash, bug bite, or healing wound; the most-heard form of this verb in a clinic.
긁어 주다 = to scratch (for someone); a casual home/couple request, with 줘 the 반말 'do it for me'.
It itched so I scratched it
The natural cause-and-effect pair: the adjective 가렵다 (itchy) feeds straight into 긁다 (scratch).
It gets itchier if you scratch
긁으면 = 'if (you) scratch'; the warning that scratching backfires, said about eczema and bites.
examples: 등을 긁었어요.
I scratched my back.
Basic frame: the itchy spot or body part takes 을/를 — 등을 긁다, 팔을 긁다.
모기 물린 데를 자꾸 긁었어요.
I kept scratching the mosquito bite.
물린 데 = 'the bitten spot' (물리다 = to get bitten); 자꾸 = 'keep (doing)', very natural for an itch you can't leave alone.
가려워도 긁으면 흉터가 남으니까 참으세요.
Even if it itches, you'll get a scar if you scratch, so hold back.
Full real-life advice: 흉터가 남다 = 'a scar remains', 참다 = to endure; 가렵다 and 긁다 appear together as always.
nuance: 긁다 is the physical act of scratching with fingernails or an object, and the itchy spot or body part takes 을/를 (등을 긁다). Its inseparable partner is the adjective 가렵다 ('to be itchy'): 가려워서 긁어요 ('it itches so I scratch') is the default chain, and the key learner distinction is exactly this — 가렵다 is the SENSATION (a descriptive adjective, 'it itches'), while 긁다 is the ACTION you take in response (a verb, 'I scratch'). Don't confuse 긁다 with the look-alike 긋다 ('to draw a line / strike a match'), a different verb entirely. Beyond skin, 긁다 has lively idioms: 복권을 긁다 (scratch a lottery ticket), 카드를 긁다 (swipe/charge a card), and 신경을 긁다 ('to get on someone's nerves', literally 'scratch the nerves'). In a medical context the negative command 긁지 마세요 ('don't scratch') is what you'll hear most.

usage: I was shivering because it was cold
The standard way to say your body shook from cold; 추워서 = 'because it's cold', the most common trigger.
떨다 also covers trembling from nerves before a test or interview; here it's the 'don't be jittery' pep talk.
The passive 떨리다 is what Koreans actually use for involuntary shaking — from cold, nerves, or low blood sugar.
덜덜 떨다 = to shake violently; the mimetic 덜덜 (teeth-chattering) makes the shivering sound vivid and native.
examples: 추워서 떨어요.
I'm shivering because it's cold.
Simplest form. 떨다 is the active verb for shaking your own body; the reason usually comes with -아서/-어서.
면접 보기 전에 너무 긴장해서 손이 떨렸어요.
I was so nervous before the interview that my hands were shaking.
Everyday nerves scenario; note the passive 떨리다 (손이 떨렸어요) for shaking you can't control — the natural choice here.
열이 나고 몸이 으슬으슬 떨려서 병원에 갔어요.
I had a fever and my body was shivering with chills, so I went to the hospital.
Real symptom report; 으슬으슬 = the shivery-chills mimetic, and 떨리다 conveys involuntary fever shakes.
nuance: 떨다 means to shake or shiver — from cold, fear, or nerves — and it is a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ regularly drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ endings: formal 떱니다 (never 떨습니다 or 떨ㅂ니다), and 떠세요. The single most important thing for a learner is the active/passive split: 떨다 is active ('to shake [something / oneself]', and you can even 떨다 your leg as a habit — 다리를 떨다), but for involuntary body shaking Koreans overwhelmingly reach for the passive 떨리다 — 손이 떨려요 ('my hands are shaking') and 몸이 떨려요 are far more natural than the active 떨어요 here. Compare with neighbors: 흔들리다 is 'to sway/wobble' (a tree, a building), while 떨다/떨리다 is fine, fast trembling of the body. To sound native, glue on mimetic adverbs — 덜덜 (hard, cold/fear shiver) and 으슬으슬 (the chilly shiver of an oncoming fever). Note the unrelated idiom 엄살 떨다 / 수선 떨다, where 떨다 means 'to make a fuss'.

Confusing 떨다/떨리다 (fast body trembling) with 흔들리다 (to sway/wobble) — a shivering body is 떨려요, but a swaying tree or rocking boat is 흔들려요.

usage: I dozed off during the meeting
A relatable confession; 회의 중에 = 'in the middle of the meeting', the prototypical wrong place to nod off.
졸음운전 (drowsy driving) is a serious road-safety phrase in Korea; 졸지 마세요 is the warning.
I dozed off for a second
깜빡 = 'for a brief moment / momentarily'; the everyday 'I nodded off just for a sec' on a couch or desk.
졸리다 = 'to feel sleepy' (the sensation), the step BEFORE 졸다 (the act); 자꾸 = 'keep (being)'.
examples: 수업 시간에 졸았어요.
I dozed off in class.
Basic frame; 졸다 is intransitive and usually pinned to a place/time you shouldn't sleep (수업 시간에 = during class).
점심 먹고 나서 자꾸 졸려서 결국 졸았어요.
After lunch I kept getting sleepy and ended up dozing off.
Shows the pair clearly: 졸리다 = 'to feel sleepy' (feeling) leads to 졸다 = 'to nod off' (act); 결국 = 'in the end'.
지하철에서 깜빡 졸다가 내릴 역을 지나쳤어요.
I dozed off for a moment on the subway and missed the stop I was supposed to get off at.
Quintessential Seoul-commuter story; V-다가 = mid-action interruption, 지나치다 = to pass by/overshoot.
nuance: 졸다 means to nod off or drift into a light doze — typically somewhere you're not supposed to, like a meeting, class, or the subway — and it is a ㄹ-stem verb, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ: formal 좁니다 (not 졸습니다). The crucial learner distinction is between 졸다 and 졸리다: 졸리다 is the adjective-like state 'to feel sleepy' (졸려요 = 'I'm drowsy', the sensation), whereas 졸다 is the verb for actually drifting off (졸았어요 = 'I nodded off', the act). It's also distinct from 자다 ('to sleep' properly, lying down for real) — 졸다 is brief, upright, involuntary micro-sleep, while 자다 is full intentional sleep. There's no Sino-Korean root; it's native Korean. It collocates with 깜빡 졸다 (doze off for a second) and feeds the compound noun 졸음 ('drowsiness'), which builds 졸음운전 (drowsy driving), plastered on every Korean highway warning sign.

usage: I feel like I'm going to throw up
A crucial phrase for food poisoning, a hangover, or motion sickness; V-(으)ㄹ 것 같다 hedges 'I feel like I might'.
I drank too much yesterday and threw up
An honest morning-after admission; 너무 마시다 = to drink too much, -아서 links cause to result.
My stomach is off / I feel queasy
속 = the stomach/gut; the softer way to say you're nauseous BEFORE you actually 토하다.
I feel a bit better after throwing up
V-고 나니까 = 'now that I've done X'; the relief that follows once it's out.
examples: 토할 것 같아요.
I think I'm going to throw up.
The bare warning you give while it's still coming on; learn this one cold for emergencies.
버스에서 차멀미가 나서 토할 뻔했어요.
I got carsick on the bus and almost threw up.
차멀미 = motion/car sickness; V-(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 = 'almost did (but didn't)', a very common near-miss pattern.
상한 걸 먹었는지 어젯밤부터 계속 토하고 설사도 해요.
I think I ate something spoiled — since last night I keep vomiting and have diarrhea too.
Full food-poisoning report; 상하다 = to go bad, -았는지 = 'whether/maybe', 설사하다 = to have diarrhea. Clinic-ready.
nuance: 토하다 is the direct, neutral verb for vomiting (Sino-Korean 吐 'spit out/vomit' + 하다, so literally 'to do a 吐'), and it's perfectly fine to use at a clinic or pharmacy. While it's already on the way up, you hedge with 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I might throw up'). Mind the register and the synonyms: the everyday softer alternative is 게우다, and for mere nausea where nothing has come out yet, Koreans say 속이 안 좋다 ('my stomach is off') or 메스껍다 / 메슥거리다 ('to feel queasy') — these describe the queasy sensation, not the act, so don't say 토해요 unless you actually vomited. (There's also the very blunt slang 게워내다/'우웩'; 토하다 itself is the safe standard.) For a doctor, pairing 토하다 with 설사하다 (diarrhea) and 열이 나다 (fever) paints the classic 식중독 (food poisoning) picture. Note the object marker: what you throw up takes 을/를 (먹은 걸 다 토했어요).

mistakes: Overusing 토하다 for mild nausea — if you only feel queasy but haven't actually vomited, say 속이 안 좋아요 or 메스꺼워요, not 토해요. 토하다 means the vomiting actually happened.
Saying 토하고 싶어요 to mean 'I feel nauseous' — that literally means 'I want to vomit' (a desire), which sounds odd. Use 토할 것 같아요 ('I feel like I'm going to') for the urge.
Forgetting 토하다 is built on 하다 — the negative is 안 토해요 / 토하지 않아요 and the past is 토했어요, conjugating like every other 하다 verb (해요 → 토해요).

english: to be sick with / to suffer from
usage: I was down with a cold for a few days
앓다 takes the illness as object (감기를); it sounds heavier and more drawn-out than just 아팠어요.
끙끙 앓다 = to agonize/groan quietly; the mimetic 끙끙 also extends to worries, not just illness.
병을 앓다 = 'to suffer from an illness'; -고 있다 marks an ongoing, chronic condition.
I came down with body aches / the whole-body flu-ache
몸살(을) 앓다 is a fixed collocation for the achy, run-down sickness from overwork or a cold.
examples: 감기를 앓았어요.
I was sick with a cold.
Core pattern: the illness is the OBJECT (감기를 앓다), unlike 아프다 which never takes an illness as object.
독감을 심하게 앓아서 일주일 동안 회사를 못 갔어요.
I had a bad case of the flu and couldn't go to work for a week.
독감 = influenza (worse than 감기); 심하게 = severely. The -아서 chains the heavy illness to its consequence.
할머니께서는 오래 병을 앓으셨지만 끝까지 의연하셨어요.
My grandmother suffered from an illness for a long time but stayed composed to the end.
Honorific -(으)시- for an elder (앓으셨다); 병을 앓다 = to suffer from a disease, a respectful, literary register.
nuance: 앓다 means to be laid low by, or suffer through, an illness over a stretch of time, and the defining grammar point is that it takes the sickness as a DIRECT OBJECT — 감기를 앓다, 독감을 앓다, 병을 앓다 — which is exactly where it parts ways with 아프다. The contrast is sharp: 아프다 is an adjective that just states something hurts or you're unwell (머리가 아파요, 몸이 아파요), whereas 앓다 is a verb meaning you actively 'go through' a named illness for a period. 앓다 also carries a heavier, more drawn-out, somewhat literary tone, so it readily extends to chronic disease and even emotional pain (마음의 병을 앓다 = 'to suffer a sickness of the heart'). The reduplicated 끙끙 앓다 paints someone groaning or quietly agonizing — over illness OR worries. Register-wise, in casual daily speech people far more often say 아팠어요; 앓다 sounds a notch more serious. It's native Korean (no hanja root). Note the modern slang 앓다 → '앓는 소리(를) 하다' meaning to whine/complain.

mistakes: Using the subject marker like 아프다 does — it's 감기를 앓다 (object 를), not 감기가 앓다. The illness is what you 'suffer through', so it takes 을/를.
Reaching for 앓다 in light, casual talk — for an everyday 'I felt sick / I was unwell', 아팠어요 is far more natural. 앓다 sounds heavy and literary, fitting flu, chronic disease, or written notes.
Trying to make 앓다 mean a single spot hurting — you can't say 머리를 앓아요 for 'my head hurts'; that's 머리가 아파요. 앓다 is for going through a whole illness (병을 앓다), not localized pain.

usage: 건강을 회복하다 = to get one's health back; the standard collocation after illness or surgery.
V-는 데 시간이 걸리다 = 'it takes time to'; an honest, reassuring line about a recovery period.
I got my condition / energy back
컨디션을 회복하다 is the everyday phrase for bouncing back to feeling normal after being run-down.
V-기(를) 바라다 = 'I hope that...'; a warmer, more formal get-well wish than 빨리 나으세요.
examples: 건강을 회복했어요.
I recovered my health.
Core pattern: 회복하다 is transitive — you recover SOMETHING (건강을/체력을/컨디션을), which takes 을/를.
수술 후에 빠르게 회복하고 있어요.
I'm recovering quickly after the surgery.
수술 후에 = after surgery; -고 있다 shows the recovery is ongoing. The clinical register fits a medical context.
푹 쉬고 영양제도 챙겨 먹으면서 체력을 회복하려고 해요.
I'm trying to get my stamina back by resting well and being sure to take supplements.
Real recovery plan; 체력 = stamina, 챙겨 먹다 = to make a point of eating, -(으)려고 하다 = 'intend to'.
nuance: 회복하다 is the somewhat formal/clinical verb for recovering, built on Sino-Korean 回復 (回 'return' + 復 'restore', i.e. 'to return-and-restore'). It is transitive — you recover a thing you had lost, taking 을/를: 건강을 회복하다 (health), 체력을 회복하다 (stamina), 컨디션을 회복하다 (condition). The register contrast with 낫다 is the key point: for an everyday 'I got better', Koreans say 나았어요 (from 낫다), which is intransitive and about an illness healing; 회복하다 sounds more clinical and suits doctors, formal recovery periods, and written sick-leave notes. When you want to say your body/condition recovered on its own without naming an object, use the passive 회복되다 (몸이 회복됐어요) rather than the active 몸이 회복했어요. Beyond the body, 회복하다 extends to non-medical comebacks — 신뢰를 회복하다 (restore trust), 경기가 회복되다 (the economy recovers). The bare noun 회복 (recovery) appears on hospital discharge papers.

Using 회복하다 for a casual 'I'm over my cold' — that's more naturally 감기가 다 나았어요 (from 낫다). 회복하다 is clinical and fits surgery, formal notes, or regaining health/stamina, not light everyday recovery.
Forgetting it's a 하다 verb when negating — the natural negatives are 회복 안 해요 / 회복 못 해요 (splitting 회복 + 하다), conjugating just like other Sino-Korean + 하다 verbs.

usage: It's hard to swallow the pills
Tell a pharmacist this and they may suggest smaller pills or syrup; V-기 힘들다 = 'hard to do'.
The classic sore-throat description; 침 = saliva, 삼킬 때 = 'when swallowing' — a precise symptom phrase.
The pharmacist's instruction for taking pills; 이랑 같이 = 'together with', casual but standard.
눈물을 삼키다 = 'to swallow one's tears'; the common figurative use you'll hear in dramas and songs.
examples: 약을 삼켰어요.
I swallowed the medicine.
Basic frame: what you swallow takes 을/를 — 약을/물을/음식을 삼키다.
알약을 물이랑 같이 삼켜요.
Swallow the tablet with water.
알약 = tablet/pill (vs 가루약 = powder medicine); the routine instruction for taking pills.
목이 부어서 음식을 삼키기가 너무 힘들어요.
My throat is swollen so it's really hard to swallow food.
Ties 삼키다 to 붓다 (to swell); 삼키기(가) 힘들다 = 'hard to swallow', a key symptom phrase for a clinic visit.
nuance: 삼키다 is the verb for swallowing — food, drink, pills, or saliva — and what goes down takes 을/를 (약을 삼키다, 침을 삼키다). It's genuinely practical at a pharmacy or clinic: 약을 삼키기 힘들어요 ('hard to swallow pills') or 침 삼킬 때 목이 아파요 ('it hurts when I swallow') pinpoint throat problems precisely. The crucial sequence partner is 씹다 ('to chew'): you 씹다 first, then 삼키다 — '씹어서 삼켜요' puts them in order — so don't use one for the other. Distinguish it also from 마시다 ('to drink/gulp a liquid continuously'); 삼키다 is the single act of sending something down the throat. It's a native Korean word (no hanja). Figuratively, 삼키다 is rich and very common: 눈물을 삼키다 (swallow one's tears), 화를 삼키다 (swallow one's anger), 비명을 삼키다 (stifle a scream) — all meaning to hold an emotion back. Safety warnings use it too: 통째로 삼키지 마세요 ('don't swallow it whole').
